PCI.BIO:
Nantakan Wongkasem joined UTRGV in 2015, and is currently an Associate Professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering. She was awarded Fred W. and Frances H Rusteberg Faculty Fellowship in 2017. She has been serving as the Department’s Graduate Coordinator since September 2020.
Dr. Wongkasem is a specialist in applied electromagnetics (EM), optics and metamaterials with expertise in designing electromagnetic-related devices (e.g., sensors, antennas, polarizers, lenses, switches, filters, EM shields, EM absorbers, etc.) and novel engineered metamaterials (e.g., chiral, near-zero refractive index, double and single negative index metamaterials, etc.), as well as optimizing the devices’ performance. She recently drew attention to ‘Electromagnetic Pollution’, an unnecessarily over-used electromagnetic radiation in nowadays wireless communication technology. In July 2021 she submitted a US provisional patent: ‘Novel Wearable Self-Powered Electromagnetic Radiation Warning Device’.
Dr. Wongkasem published 64 refereed research papers and holds 11 awarded and 1 pending patents.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Self-Awareness Electromagnetic Pollution Monitor:  Mobile Self-Powered Electromagnetic Radiation Warning Platforms
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Overview: Electromagnetic (EM) radiation or electromagnetic field (EMF) from communications and electronic devices, networks, systems and base stations has drawn concern due to excessive global usage with increasing radiation power and operating frequency level. Nowadays multi-billions of wireless devices and their immense unused residual EM radiations linger all around. In this research, we tag these unwanted and needless EM radiations as ‘Electromagnetic Pollution’. Numerous publications stress that the EM radiation from certain frequency ranges of particular devices can harm specific human organs and tissues, resulting in distinct symptoms.
This research focuses on developing the first mobile self-powered EM radiation warning platform. We aim to perfect the EM radiation receiving system, and the self-powered feature, stressing the platform’s accuracy and reliability. The frequency of interest starts from the most widely used wireless communication (e.g., Wi-Fi, 4G LTE, Bluetooth, Zigbee) frequency at 2.4GHz, 5G HF (High Frequency), 3.1-4.2GHz, up to the new 5G mmW-hot spots at 28GHz. To help expedite progress in this area, our objective involves fabrication and thorough evaluation of all interconnected EM components. Explicitly, we propose the construction of a highly efficient EM radiation capturing system, in which the EM radiation is precisely detected, captured, recorded, and evaluated in a broad multi-band wireless communication frequency range within a specific time interval. The EM output from the EM radiation receiving system will be directly rectified to utilize the whole platform, making the platform self-powered and mobile, emphasizing the platforms’ reliability.

Intellectual Merit: The major innovation of the proposed work is the design of the first mobile self-powered EM radiation waring platform, which holds significant promise in preventing the future jeopardy of exponentially expanding EM radiation pollution. The EM radiation will be continually detected, stored, and evaluated by a mobile EM radiation warning device worn by any individual users based on any fluctuating environments. Hence, we can all acknowledge our specific EM exposure risk and find our ways to reduce the radiation reception.

Broader Impacts: This work addresses the importance of EM pollution and proposes to develop the first mobile self-powered electromagnetic radiation warning platform, which operates much like the warning light on the dashboard of a car. When flashing, it lets you know that it is time to be alert. We aim to introduce and publicize the EM radiation warning platform as one of the mandatory alarming systems, similar to fire alarms, carbon monoxide and smoke detectors. This work will provide a fundamental understanding of the design, fabrication and testing of self-awareness mobile EM radiation warning platform, which will promote research and engineering efforts leading to significant advances in future EM radiation pollution monitoring.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Development of Metamaterial-Inspired Sensing Platforms with Multiple Reactivity  for Toxic Heavy Metal Trace Detection
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Overview: Arsenic, Mercury, Lead, and Cadmium are among the 10 chemicals of major public health concern listed by the World Health Organization (WHO). Symptoms and physical findings associated with heavy metal poisoning vary according to the absorbed dose or the metal accumulated in the soft tissues of human body, the rate of emission and duration of exposure. These metallic elements are listed as carcinogens (Sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC)) and are considered systemic toxicants known to induce multiple organ damage, even at lower levels of exposure. Heavy metal pollution and contamination can originate in a multitude of sources (e.g., soil, water, food, dust, etc.). Our research addresses metal toxicity concerns by developing alternative, simple, yet effective and green ways to trace and monitor toxic heavy metals.
This is a 2-year project focusing on the development of a new generation of heavy metal sensors. We aim to explore and develop the foundations of an improved alternative to trace-level ion in situ heavy metal sensors, introducing on-site, instantaneous (real-time), ultra-sensitive, contactless, toxic heavy metal sensing platforms. Uniquely designed metamaterial sensing enhancers will be integrated with designated electromagnetic wave excitations/interactions to create multiple reactivity in order to boost the detecting sensitivity and accuracy of the sensors for specific toxic heavy metals.

Intellectual Merit: The major innovation of the proposed work is the complementary engagement of GHz wave interaction, antennas, and fundamental metamaterial design analysis to create a remarkable new generation of on-site, real-time, ultra-sensitive, and contactless toxic heavy metal sensing platforms with optimal multiple reactivity, and green process, which holds significant promise for the future of heavy metal sensors.

Broader Impacts: This work will lead to the discovery of novel sensing concepts that will narrow down or even close the gap between the laboratory and the environmental field, by developing an on-site (stationary and/or portable) real-time sensing platform, with the ability to monitor the toxic heavy contamination in environmental systems. This new generation of toxic heavy metal sensors will not only address all the cons of the existing ones (i.e., laboratory-based restrictions, exposure, limit of detection, waste, etc.), but they will also be rapid, simple and highly accurate. This work will provide a fundamental understanding of the design, fabrication and testing of heavy metal sensors, which will promote research and engineering efforts leading to significant advances in new generation GHz wave interaction sensing platforms.

CONGRANT.TITLE: NRT-QISE: NRT Quantum Information Science and Engineering Innovative Program (QISEP) at Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Quantum information science is a rapidly developing field spanning physics, chemistry, engineering, and computer science, with the potential to generate breakthrough technologies for communication, sensing, and computing that exploit the quantum behavior of light and matter. The goal of the NRT Quantum Information Science and Engineering Innovative Program (QISEP) at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is to prepare the next generation of scientists and engineers to meet the growing demand for quantum-capable workers. The program will cross traditional boundaries between fields and introduce a multidisciplinary graduate curriculum emphasizing the connections between fundamental and applied science, theory and experiment, and thereby preparing young researchers for successful careers in academia, industry, and government. The educational component of this NRT program is a new degree track in Quantum Information Science & Engineering (QISE) available to Physics, Chemistry, and Electrical Engineering majors. The complementary training component will empower cohorts of NRT students to collaborate within and communicate among three major areas of research denoted Quantum Research Clusters (Solid State Qubits, Photon Qubits, and Superconducting Qubits in Quantum Electrodynamics Circuits). Summer internship opportunities with partners including X – The Moonshot Factory, Honeywell Quantum Solutions, and the University of Houston will offer trainees the chance to work side-by-side with some of the most talented researchers in QISE. Integrated training in communication, ethics, and project management will help NRT students develop into engaged, responsible, and productive members of the scientific community. This NRT program will ultimately provide access to QISE expertise and research facilities for 40 master’s students (25 supported by this grant and 15 supported by participating departments), who will gain marketable experience by training with modern instrumentation and software in an interdisciplinary research environment. Moreover, approximately 150 more UTRGV graduate students will participate in the program by attending NRT QISEP seminars and symposia. Keywords: quantum information; qubits; quantum computing; quantum sensing; nanotechnology; nanophotonics; metamaterials; Track 2.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Development of Microwave Metamaterial-Inspired Sensors with Multiple-Band Reactivity for Mercury Contamination Detection
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Journal of Electromagnetic Waves and Applications
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Alternative contactless metamaterial-inspired microwave sensors, composed of a multi-band omnidirectional bowtie antenna and metamaterials, are developed to detect and identify mercury, one of the most widespread toxic heavy metals, in the C-band and S-band, using reflection coefficients. A multi-negative refractive index band metamaterial is specifically designed as a sensing enhancer, where the multi bands can effectively trigger the electromagnetic properties, as well as enhance the differentiation between the mercury samples. The geometry of the metamaterial and its arrangement and orientation are optimized to reach the system highest sensitivity. The proposed sensors were tested on mercury traces of various volumes and weights. Our study has shown that the electromagnetic responses of the mercury in the microwave range are nonlinear, yet predictable. Six distinguishable resonances generated while testing the samples specify the capability of identifying the mercury amount, which can effectively trace mercury contamination in water and seawater.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Metal Discovery by Highly Sensitive Microwave Multi-Band Metamaterial-Inspired Sensors
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Abstract—A simple, compact, contactless, and high sensitivity metamaterial-inspired sensor has been developed to detect and classify precious transition metals in the S- and C-band regime, using reflection coefficients. A multi-band metamaterial, quadruple concentric circular split ring resonator, is specifically designed as a sensing enhancer, where the additional bands can effectively trigger the electromagnetic properties, as well as enhance the differentiation between the testing metal samples. The proposed sensor was tested on precious transition metals, silver, platinum, and gold thin slabs of various thicknesses, from0.5 μm to 3mm. Five resonances were established in the frequency range of 2–8GHz. Distinguishable frequency responses generated from different metal samples at those five resonances specify the capability of classifying the metal contents and thicknesses.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Electromagnetic Pollution Alert: Microwave Radiation and Absorption in Human Organs and Tissues
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Electromagnetic radiation from communication and electronic devices, networks, systems and base stations has drawn concern due to excessive global usage with increasing power and operating frequency level. Numerous previous researches only focus on how the radiation from certain frequency ranges of particular devices could harm specific human organs and tissues, resulting in distinct symptoms. In this research, electromagnetic propagation and properties in fourteen human organs and tissues were analyzed and investigated based on the organs and tissues’ electromagnetic and mechanical parameters, and chemical composition. Counting the organs and tissues as electromagnetic materials, their permittivity and conductivity, computed by a 4-Cole-Cole mode, directly respective to the operating frequency, are interrelated to wave behavior and hence influence the organs’ response.
Tests were conducted in 1GHz to 105GHz system settings, covering most microwave frequency uses: 2.4GHz of 4G-LTE, WiFi, Bluetooth, ZigBee, and the 5G ranges: 28GHz of 5G-mmW and 95GHz of 5G-IoT. Trial human organs and tissues were placed in the wave propagation direction of 2.4GHz and 28GHz dipole antennas, and a waveguide port operating from 95-105GHz. The quantitative data on the effects of 5G penetration and dissipation within human tissues are presented. The absorbance in all organs and tissues is significantly higher as frequency increases. As the wave enters the organ-tissue model, the wavelength is shortened due to the high organ-tissue permittivity. Skin-Bone-Brain layer simulation results demonstrate that both electric and magnetic fields vanish before passing the brain layer at all three focal frequencies of 2.4GHz, 28GHz, and 100GHz.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Chlorophyll-Inspired Tunable Metamaterials with Multi-Negative Refractive Index Bands: The Porphyrin Ring and Hydrophobic Tail Effect
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Tunable negative electromagnetic properties: permittivity, permeability, and refractiveindex, in mimic Chlorophyll metamaterial structures in the X- and Ku-band regimes are theoreticallyand numerically demonstrated. A very broad negative permeability covering the majority of the X- andKu bands, from 8GHz to 16GHz, is observed, while five negative permittivity bands are found withinthe same range. The two aforementioned properties result in a broad, greater than 25% bandwidth,low-loss negative-refractive index transmission band. These negative electromagnetic properties can beeffectively tailored within the low-loss multi-transmission and the high-loss multi-absorption bands inthe operating frequency range by modifying the structure’s tiller part or the artificial hydrophobic orPhytol tail. By focusing either on the transmission or the absorption bands, these passive always-onbio-inspired metamaterials could be utilized in microelectronic, communication and photonic, and opticdevices.
